power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: In the absence of face-valid indicators, particularly in children, liability to substance use/addiction requires quantification.
The Transmissible Liability Index (TLI) was developed for this purpose by employing a high-risk design and item response theory and quantifies this liability in childhood, before substance exposure.
Because the TLI places liability to substance use disorder on a common scale, it can also facilitate harmonization across datasets collected from different populations.
This study extends prior research by examining genetic and environmental contributions to TLI and its relationship with liability to the initiation of licit and illicit substance use.
The study utilizes data of TLI, and substance use tracked from age 11 to age 25 from longitudinal twin studies in Virginia and Minnesota.

Results showed that TLI is highly heritable and that substance use initiation (SUI) reflected a mixture of genetic and shared environmental influences varying across substance classes, consistent with the principle that initiation is more environmentally sensitive than progression.

The genetic correlations between childhood TLI and lifetime SUI are consistently stronger than the environmental correlations and support a developmental interpretation in which early heritable liability manifests in SUI and, further downstream, in disorder.

In addition to confirming TLI's high heritability, predictive validity, and utility for dataset harmonization, it supports the feasibility of identifying high-and average-resistance samples, to be used for selecting specific indicators of resistance to substance use/addiction.

This study suggests that a specific set of behavioral characteristics assessed in childhood and adolescence is correlated with the initiation of substances such as alcohol, nicotine, cannabis and illicit drugs partly because of the same genes influencing both.
These characteristics could be used to predict who will likely initiate substances.
Substance use frequently leads to substance use disorders (SUDs) (i.e., addiction), characterized by persistent use despite various negative consequences.
Severe consequences due to substance use do not require the diagnostic threshold of SUD to be met.
Therefore, any substance use behavior presents a significant public health and social hazard (Vanyukov et al., 2023).

text.text: The diagnostic categorization of SUDs arbitrarily dichotomizes the continuous latent (unobserved directly) trait of liability to substance use that underlies variation in the behaviors pertaining to substances, including those that represent asymptomatic/"normal" phenotypes.
Further, the prevalence of substance use behaviors is higher than that of SUDs.

Consequently, understanding the etiology of SUDs may also benefit from subclinical phenotypes which include substance use behaviors that precede a diagnosis of SUDs as well as the liability underlying SUDs.

These characteristics were assessed by items comprising psychological and diagnostic questionnaires, reflecting the behavioral foundations of common (non-specific to particular substances) liability to substance use/addiction (Vanyukov et al., 2012).

text.text: These properties have been replicated in two twin samples, supporting the robustness of TLI's genetic architecture across studies.

Further, the genetic component of TLI assessed in childhood accounts for the entire phenotypic relationship between TLI and subsequent SUD outcomes in adolescence and young adulthood, with no unique environmental factors shared between them.
These results validate TLI as a measure of transmissible -primarily heritable -SUD liability in children and support its utility for early-age genetic and mechanistic studies of addiction.

Importantly, because IRT places individual scores on a common metric irrespective of sample and subset of items used, TLI can also be scored across independently collected datasets: applying the CEDAR-derived item parameters to MTFS data yielded scores closely convergent with those obtained from calibration within MTFS itself (r = 0.91, Spearman ρ = 0.95), with equivalent prediction of adult diagnosis (Vanyukov et al., 2015).

text.text: SUI (i.e., first engagement of substance use at any point in the lifetime) is a common and important behavior in the development of SUD since any substance use behavior is contingent on having started use.

In 2018, the prevalence of initiation for alcohol, cannabis, and tobacco was between 13.4% -26.3% in American adolescents ages 12-17 and 51.5% -79.7% among young adults ages 18-25 (Volkow et al., 2021).

text.text: The role of genetic and environmental factors on SUI varies across drugs and across the life course.

Twin studies in adolescents aged 12-19 consistently report that additive genetic (15-75%) and shared environmental factors (30-84%) account for a substantial proportion of the variance in the liability to initiation of nicotine and alcohol (Huizink et al., 2010; Kochvar et al., 2023; Maes et al., 1999 Maes et al., , 2017;; Prom-Wormley et al., 2021).

For initiation of any illicit drug (i.e., cannabis, cocaine, stimulants, sedatives, hallucinogens, and opiates), genetic contributions ranged from 15% to 61%, whereas shared environmental contributions accounted for 32% to 59% of the variance (Agrawal & Lynskey, 2006; Zellers et al., 2024).

Variance due to additive genetic effects for initiation was higher in females for conventional cigarettes (females = 32-95%, males = 19-24%), alcohol (females = 21-48%, males = 1-29%), and cannabis (females = 18-72%, males = 22-44%).

text.text: A combined dataset of twins provides additional opportunities to obtain more precise estimates of model parameters, extended evaluation of sex differences, as well as detailed analyses of various aspects of substance use in their relationship with the childhood measure of liability and its further validation as a tool for identifying high-resistance individuals.
This article reports the results of biometric genetic analyses of the TLI and SUI in the harmonized twin data from two studies.
Data from two samples of male and female same-sex monozygotic (MZ) and dizygotic (DZ) twins reared together, were assessed across adolescence into young adulthood in Virginia and Minnesota.
The Virginia sample included opposite-sex twins.
All procedures in the contributing studies were approved by the Institutional Review Boards of Virginia Commonwealth University and the University of Minnesota.
Written informed consent was obtained from parents or guardians, and assent from participating children, at each assessment; participants provided their own consent upon reaching the age of majority.

Six variables representing lifetime SUI for specific substances (nicotine, alcohol or cannabis) or a group of substances (illicit drug use without or with cannabis, any substance use) were studied.

text.text: Univariate Twin Models Standard univariate ACE models were fitted to twin data to quantify genetic and environmental contributions to individual differences in TLI and SUI.
These models partition variance in additive genetic (A), common environmental (C) and nonshared (or unique) environmental (E; including measurement error) factors (e.g., Neale & Cardon, 1992).

text.text: Likelihood ratio tests and Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) were used to select the best fitting models.
Whilst models for continuous data were fit to TLI scores, a threshold model was assumed for the binary SUI measures to allow partitioning of the underlying liability to initiate substances.
Prior to ACE model fitting, we evaluated model assumptions in saturated models.
We further tested whether variance components could be equated by sample and sex.
To evaluate the sources of covariance between TLI and SUI, we fitted a correlated factors model which quantifies the ACE sources of (co)variance to the joint continuous (TLI) and binary (SUI) data.
These models assessed the degree to which the observed covariance between TLI and SUI can be explained by genetic and environmental factors shared between them.
We present genetic (rA), shared (rC) and unique (rE) environmental correlations from the joint continuous-binary model (Figure 1).

text.text: To account for the possibility that TLI (variable x) has a direct causal effect on SUI (variable y) (or vice-versa), we also tested causal models where TLI was a cause of SUI (byx), and where the causal direction was reversed such that SUI caused TLI (bxy).

We thus took a more agnostic approach by testing all possible identified models with up to three out of the five possible sources of covariance (rA, rC, rE, byx, bxy) and used multimodel inference methods to summarize the goodness-of-fit of the models and to calculate weights used in model averaging to obtain the 'best' estimates of the parameters of interest (Kirkpatrick et al., 2015; Maes et al., 2021).

text.text: TLI was significantly higher in males versus females in both samples.
The prevalences of tobacco, cannabis and illicit drug initiation were significantly higher in males in both samples.
Prevalence for alcohol and any substance initiation did not differ significantly by sex within either sample.
For TLI, DZ correlations were approximately half the MZ correlations, consistent with substantial additive genetic contributions.

For the SUI variables, DZ twin correlations were generally higher than half the MZ correlations, suggesting contributions of both additive genetic and shared environmental factors to variation in liability of substance initiation (see Supplemental Table 4).

text.text: Model assumptions, including equality of means/thresholds and variances by twin order and zygosity were met for each variable when tested separately by sample.
Since only the Virginia sample included opposite sex twin pairs, we fitted a univariate sex limitation model to the TLI data.
Neither qualitative nor quantitative sex differences were significant for TLI.

The best fitting model was an AE model, resulting in a heritability estimate of 0.72 (95% CI = 0.67; 0.75) and the residual E variance component estimated at 0.28 (95% CI = 0.25; 0.33) for TLI when variance component parameters were equated across sex.

In the Minnesota sample, an AE model was also the best fitting model including significant quantitative sex differences in variance components, with heritability estimates of 0.74 (95% CI = 0.70; 0.78) for males and 0.59 (95% CI = 0.52; 0.64) for females.
When combining the VTSABD and MTFS samples, estimates for the AE variance components were statistically different by sex and between samples (Table 2).

text.text: Heritability estimates of liability to substance use ranged from 0.17 to 0.28 for nicotine initiation, -0.02 to 0.46 for alcohol initiation, 0.17 to 0.41 for cannabis initiation, 0.34 to 0.57 for initiation of illicit drugs (not including cannabis), 0.19 to 0.30 for drug use initiation (cannabis or other drugs) and -0.17 to 0.48 for initiation of any substance.

Estimates of contributions of shared environmental factors to SUI liability were almost consistently higher than heritability estimates and ranged from 0.47 to 0.71 for nicotine, from 0.41 to 0.90 for alcohol, from 0.43 to 0.64 for cannabis, from 0.10 to 0.53 for other illicit drugs, from 0.32 to 0.53 for use of any drugs and from 0.40 to 0.96 for any substance use.
Unique environmental factors, which include measurement error, explained mostly between 10 and 25% of the variance in liability to SUI.
We opted to present estimates of variance components from the full ACE sex limitation model to provide more consistent comparisons across substances, sex and sample.
In each case, at least one of the sources of familial resemblance (A or C) contributed significantly to the liability of substance initiation.

The few instances of negative estimates of the additive genetic variance component, for alcohol and any substance initiation, reflect cases where the respective variance component can be dropped from the model without significant loss of model fit.

Supplementary analyses constraining twin correlations and variance components across sex and sample, while allowing for main effects of sex and sample, confirmed the pattern of results (see Supplemental Table 5).

text.text: We first fitted ACE correlated factors models to TLI and each of the six SUI variables to estimate the role of genetic and environmental factors to the variance and covariance of TLI and SUI.
The results for the variance decomposition of the two variables mirrored those of the univariate analyses, as expected.
We thus focus here on estimates of the genetic and environmental correlations between TLI and initiation of each substance (Table 3).

text.text: As shared environmental factors did not contribute significantly to the variance of TLI, in contrast to their contributions to SUI liability, we could not estimate rC's.
In addition, for variables with negative estimates of heritability, rA's were not estimated.
The estimated rA's were, with few exceptions, consistently higher than rE's.

The highest rA's were observed between TLI and initiation of nicotine (0.27 to 0.59), followed by any drug use (0.28 to 0.32), illicit use excluding cannabis (0.24 to 0.31) and cannabis (0.23 to 0.24) in males, whilst the rA's between TLI and alcohol initiation or any substance use were not significantly different from zero.
In contrast, estimates of rE's showed the highest values between TLI and alcohol or any substance initiation.
Estimates were broadly consistent across samples with the largest discrepancy for correlations between TLI and nicotine initiation.
The pattern of rA's between TLI and SUI in females was similar to that in males but estimates were lower in both samples. rE's were low and non-significant in both samples as well as across sex.

As covariation between TLI and SUI could also arise from direct causal effects between TLI and SUI, we extended analyses to testing all possible identified models including one or both causal paths (b>: from TLI to SUI, or b<: from SUI to TLI) and/or any of the possible confounding paths (rA or rE in this case) (see Figure 2 and Supplemental Table 6).

Estimates of causal paths from TLI to SUI were generally higher than reverse causation paths from SUI to TLI in males, but rather variable or in the reverse direction in females.
These trends are strongest for nicotine and any illicit drug initiation and for males compared to females.

text.text: This study extends prior research on the TLI by examining its genetic and environmental architecture and relationship with SUI.
The study was conducted in the VTSABD and the MTFS twin samples, the harmonization of which was enabled by the TLI.

Results elaborate upon previous evidence for TLI's high heritability and predictive validity, demonstrate the feasibility of IRT-based dataset harmonization across studies, confirm that variation in SUI is influenced by a combination of genetic and shared environmental factors, and establish that the genetic link between childhood TLI and initiation of substance use is consistently stronger than the environmental link across most substances.
The results strengthen the case for TLI as a quantitative, early-childhood index of transmissible SUD liability.
This study demonstrates that TLI can be successfully used to calibrate across datasets from different populations using an anchor-item IRT approach.

By identifying 13 common items across CEDAR, VTSABD, and MTFS (29% of original TLI item pool), sufficient to serve as a psychometric bridge, TLI scores were placed on a common metric that minimized instrument-related and study-design variance.
This follows established principles of IRT-based harmonization, where invariant anchor items enable linking of nonequivalent groups onto a shared latent scale (Gibbons et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This follows established principles of IRT-based harmonization, where invariant anchor items enable linking of nonequivalent groups onto a shared latent scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Gibbons et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The replication of the TLI heritability estimates and the structural consistency of bivariate TLI-SUI results across samples further validate the approach.

As the field increasingly relies on large multi-site consortia for molecular genetic studies, the ability to harmonize a childhood liability index across diverse studies substantially expands the scope of applicable samples (Conway et al. 2010).

text.text: Results are consistent with a previous study from CEDAR and closely parallel those reported in the MTFS alone using IRT-derived TLI scores (Vanyukov et al., 2015), a sum-of-z-score approach for TLI items (Hicks et al., 2012), and with the heritability of the broader externalizing spectrum (Krueger et al. 2002).

text.text: The qualitative conclusion of high heritability without shared environmental contribution held across both studies, as did estimates in males.

In contrast, in females, statistically significant quantitative differences in variance components between the VTSABD and MTFS, with heritability estimates higher in the former, warrant consideration.
While these differences cannot be explained by higher liability in the VTSABD sample (the rates of initiation are not substantially different), several factors may contribute to these differences.

First, the two studies were conducted in different geographic regions, and environmental shifts in substance availability, social norms, and parental monitoring practices can alter the relative magnitude of genetic and environmental variance (Dick et al., 2007).
text.formatted: First, the two studies were conducted in different geographic regions, and environmental shifts in substance availability, social norms, and parental monitoring practices can alter the relative magnitude of genetic and environmental variance <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Dick et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: When shared environmental variance is systematically higher in one region -for example, due to greater homogeneity in community-level influences -heritability estimates will be correspondingly lower.

Second, developmental timing differences may play a role, as heritability of externalizing traits is known to strengthen across adolescence alongside their increasing expression (Iacono et al., 1999), and the two studies assessed twins at somewhat different ages and across different numbers of waves.
text.formatted: Second, developmental timing differences may play a role, as heritability of externalizing traits is known to strengthen across adolescence alongside their increasing expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Iacono et al., 1999)</ref>, and the two studies assessed twins at somewhat different ages and across different numbers of waves.

text.text: Third, residual measurement non-equivalence cannot be excluded: despite the IRT harmonization, non-anchor items in each sample may cover different portions of the liability continuum with different precision, and differential measurement error is absorbed into the E component, which may artificially deflate heritability in the sample with noisier measurement.
These explanations are not mutually exclusive, and consistency of the qualitative results across samples suggests that between-study differences reflect degree rather than kind.

Quantitative sex differences in TLI heritability, with higher estimates in males than females observed in MFTS, replicate prior observations (Vanyukov et al., 2009 (Vanyukov et al., , 2015) ) and are consistent with a pattern seen across substance use phenotypes and externalizing traits (Krueger et al., 2002).

text.text: The mechanisms are unclear but may reflect the greater prevalence and heritability of externalizing and disinhibitory traits in males, or genuine sexspecific pathways to addiction liability.

Despite DIF adjustment, residual quantitative sex differences suggest that some portion of TLI variance is due to sex-specific genetic or environmental factors, a question warranting further investigation in larger samples.
In line with an extensive literature on substance use twin studies, heritability estimates for lifetime SUI were in most cases, lower than for SUDs.
Across substances, shared environment accounted for a larger proportion of SUI variance than additive genetic factors, replicating previous results (Fowler et al., 2007; Maes et al., 1999).

text.text: In that study, the variance for adult SUD diagnosis in the MTFS was dominated by shared environmental factors, with a smaller additive genetic component.

The present results extend this pattern earlier in the SUD trajectory: across substances, SUI showed similarly prominent shared environment, while the contribution of additive genetic factors increases as the phenotype moves from initiation toward disorder.

Heritability estimates for alcohol initiation were particularly low and, in some cells, nominally negative, reflecting well-documented results indicating that variation in whether one ever tries alcohol is almost entirely driven by social and family environment, with genetic factors becoming more influential for later stages of consumption and problem development, i.e., higher liability levels (Maes et al., 2017; Verhulst et al., 2015).

text.text: The few instances of negative estimates of variance components likely reflect cases where the respective variance component can be dropped without significant loss of model fit.

The bivariate analyses show a theoretically coherent pattern: genetic correlations between childhood TLI and lifetime SUI were positive across most substances and substantially higher than the corresponding unique environmental correlations, consistent with TLI's rationale as an index of the transmissible -primarily genetic -component of SUD liability.

These results complement the bivariate results reported previously in the MTFS (Vanyukov et al., 2015), where the genetic variance of TLI accounted for more than half of the genetic variance in adult SUD diagnosis, with the genetic correlation accounting for the entire phenotypic relationship between the two measures.

text.text: The present results address an earlier point in the same phenotypic development and show that the genetic signal from childhood TLI is already detectable at the initiation stage, before disorder has developed.
The substance-specific pattern of genetic correlations is informative and broadly consistent across the two samples.
The highest rA was observed for nicotine initiation, followed by any drug use initiation, illicit drugs excluding cannabis, and cannabis.

Estimates for rA's of alcohol initiation and any substance initiation were unstable and, in some cases, hit the lower or upper bound, likely resulting from the very high prevalence of alcohol initiation and the very low or negative heritability estimates for these measures.

The gradient of rAs closely mirrors the known gradient in heritability of initiation across substances -nicotine and illicit drug use share more genetic architecture with the externalizing/disinhibitory spectrum that TLI indexes than does normative alcohol initiation (Agrawal & Lynskey, 2006).

text.text: A notable result is that rA values for nicotine in the VTSABD are comparable to those reported previously (Vanyukov et al., 2015) for adult SUD diagnosis.

text.text: This is at first sight surprising, since disorder is more severe, and liability to it is more heritable relative to initiation.

It suggests that the genetic connection between childhood TLI and nicotine, as well as illicit drug involvement, is already near its maximum at the initiation stage, with the transition to disorder phenotypes adding substance-specific variance rather than amplifying the shared genetic signal from TLI.

The somewhat lower rA values in the MTFS for several substances likely reflect the between-sample differences in TLI heritability discussed above, particularly in females, where a lower heritable variance in TLI constrains the maximum possible genetic correlation with any outcome.
In general, since TLI is designed to index liability to adult illicit SUD, this may also suggest that smoking has become almost as nonnormative as illicit substance use.
The non-significant and near-zero rA for alcohol initiation and any substance initiation deserves attention.

Alcohol initiation is common -over 80% in both samples -and so dominated by shared environmental influences (C = 0.78 in males and 0.71 in females) that the heritable variance available to correlate with TLI's genetic component is minimal in the VTSABD.

The between-sample and between-sex differences in alcohol rA could be attributable to sampling variability and statistical imprecision, given that rA estimates for lowheritability-particularly for binary traits-may be imprecise and unstable (Neale & Cardon, 1992).

text.text: More broadly, results suggest that TLI's genetic reach extends to alcohol involvement more strongly at the disorder stage than at initiation.
The rE values between TLI and SUI were generally small and non-significant but showed a substantively interesting pattern.
In males, rE was positive for most substances in both samples.
The highest values were for precisely the phenotypes with the highest shared environmental variance and lowest heritability.

This suggests that in males, some unique environmental experiences independently co-vary with both the behavioral precursors captured by TLI and the likelihood of initiating substance use, most plausibly early behavioral problems leading to environments where substances are encountered, independent of the heritable liability pathway.

In females, rE values were near zero or negative across most substances and samples, suggesting that the unique environmental factors associated with higher TLI scores do not co-vary positively with SUI.
The rA estimates were most consistent across the VTSABD and MTFS for cannabis and illicit drugs excluding cannabis.
These data further support the validity of the IRT harmonization.

Taken together with data for SUD diagnosis (Vanyukov et al., 2015) and for adolescent substance abuse composite scores (Hicks et al., 2012), these results provide converging evidence across three different SUD-related outcomes and two independent twin cohorts that the genetic component of childhood TLI systematically predicts substance involvement across the developmental continuum, with the strength of the genetic connection reflecting the heritability of liabilities to substance use-related developmental outcomes.

text.text: Extending the correlated-factors approach to causal modeling, the model-averaging results suggested that the direction of effect predominantly runs from TLI to SUI in males, with higher causal path estimates in that direction than the reverse.

This is consistent with the developmental logic underlying TLI's construction and with prior bivariate results (Vanyukov et al., 2015), where the temporal ordering of childhood TLI and adult SUD diagnosis was interpreted in explicitly directional ontogenetic terms: TLI measures liability at an earlier developmental stage, and its genetic variance propagates forward to influence liability as indexed by the later diagnosis.

text.text: Because TLI was assessed in childhood while SUI aggregates subsequent waves, a path from SUI to TLI is not developmentally interpretable; the female estimates are more plausibly attributable to low heritability and threshold measurement of the binary SUI variables than to reverse causation.

The present causal modeling extends this framework to SUI as an intermediate outcome, in line with longitudinal evidence that childhood externalizing behavior and behavioral disinhibition prospectively predict substance use onset (Iacono et al., 1999; King et al., 2004; Samek et al., 2017; Vanyukov et al., 2015) and that polygenic scores for behavioral disinhibition in childhood forecast later substance use across multiple substances (Schaefer et al., 2023).

text.text: A primary motivation for this research is the identification of high-resistance individuals -those at the low end of the SUD liability distribution -who can serve as a contrast population for the discovery of resistance factors, the poorly understood counterpart of risk, as well as indicators specifically of the resistance aspect of liability (Vanyukov et al., 2016 (Vanyukov et al., , 2023)).

text.text: Resistance factors may have greater translation potential than risk factors, because it is those factors that prevent a disorder on the background of the ubiquity and ready availability of psychoactive/addictive substances, from licit to increasingly decriminalized illicit ones.

Nonetheless, it is risk factors that continue to be the common focus of research: e.g., research efforts are applied to the mechanisms of return to opioid use rather than those of persistent abstinence (Luo et al., 2024).

text.text: Examples of implementation of a resistance approach are rare in general and in substance use in particular.
One reason for that is the prevailing "disease model," which by definition targets the risk aspect.

In addition, behavioral traits are "complex" meaning that variation in them is determined by numerous genetic and nongenetic factors rather than by a single factor such as exposure/non-exposure to an environmental agent or in monogenic traits.

In complex traits, including substance use and the multifactorially inherited, and thus likely normally distributed liabilities to behavioral/psychiatric disorders, the absence of disorder or of its symptoms does not necessarily correspond to high resistance to it.
As unaffected individuals comprise 90-95% of the population, their average liability is close to the population average.
The identification of genuinely high-resistance individuals requires a continuous liability metric such as the TLI.
The present results strengthen the empirical foundation for this approach in several respects.
Confirming that TLI variance is predominantly genetic validates TLI scores as reflecting heritable differences.
Establishing that TLI is genetically correlated with SUI across multiple substance classes confirms that TLI covers the same liability dimension underlying the outcomes of interest.

Demonstrating feasibility of cross-study harmonization indicates that low-TLI individuals can be identified from pooled existing datasets, providing the statistical power needed to characterize a phenotypically unusual group.
This supports the ongoing Resist!
research program (Prom-Wormley et al., 2022; Vanyukov et al., 2023).

text.text: Several limitations should be noted.

Residual between-study heterogeneity in TLI variance components, despite IRT harmonization, may reflect genuine population differences, cohort effects, or residual measurement non-equivalence that the anchor-item approach could not fully eliminate.

SUI was coded as a lifetime binary variable, which does not capture timing or developmental context of first use; prior research indicates that age at first use carries important genetic information and independently predicts SUD risk (Richmond-Rakerd et al., 2016).

text.text: The samples are predominantly of European ancestry.

Prior work has noted that TLI items selected in European-American samples may not perform equivalently in African-American samples, where transmissibility of SUD liability may be differently structured (Vanyukov et al., 2009).

text.text: This study demonstrates high heritability, predictive validity, and suitability of the TLI for cross-study harmonization to generalize across two independent longitudinal twin cohorts.

Quantitative between-sample differences in heritability estimates most plausibly reflect cohort, regional, developmental timing, and residual measurement factors rather than fundamental differences in genetic architecture.

SUI reflects a mixture of genetic and shared environmental influences varying across substance classes, consistent with the principle that initiation is more environmentally sensitive than progression.

Genetic connections between childhood TLI and lifetime SUI are consistently stronger than environmental connections and support a developmental interpretation in which early heritable liability manifests in SUI and, further downstream, in disorder.

These results validate TLI as a tool for quantifying the full range of SUD liability -including both risk and resistance -and support its application in identifying high-resistance samples as a complement to the established high-risk research paradigm.
